blocks.en: Hello, young explorers, and welcome back to Michael's Morning Listening!
Today, both of our stars are champions of hide-and-seek.
One hid in a museum for almost a hundred years.
The other hid in front of everybody's eyes for forty years.
Nobody had to find them in the wild.
Somebody just had to look at them.

title: 狮身人面像的鳄鱼邻居

blocks.en: Our first story begins in Egypt, beside the famous Sphinx.
The Great Sphinx of Giza, lion-bodied and king-faced, was carved from a ridge of limestone, rock that was once a warm sea floor.
Inside those rocks, scientists have recognised a crocodile never named before.
The animal, Herugavialis cairensis, lived forty-five million years ago.
It was a gavial, a crocodile with a long, thin snout for snapping up fish, and a curved ridge circled each of its eyes.
Our hero is a skull.
Collectors dug it out of the Mokattam rocks in the nineteen twenties.
It travelled to a German museum and slept for almost a hundred years.
Its label named a known crocodile, and nobody questioned it for decades.
Then an international team took a closer look.
They slid the skull into a CT scanner, a machine that lets doctors and scientists peek inside objects without breaking them open.
After comparing three hundred details, the team concluded: this was not the crocodile on the label.
It was a new genus, a branch that science had missed.
They named it after Heru, a god linked with the Sphinx.
And like the Sphinx, it is missing the tip of its snout.
Our second treasure was hiding in plain sight in a university collection in Germany.
It looks like a woodlouse that swallowed a growth potion: hard scaly shell, many legs.
It is a giant isopod, a deep-sea cousin of the tiny pill bugs, only this one is thirty-two centimetres long.
Scientists call monsters this size colossogiants.
It came from the Caribbean Sea, near Puerto Rico, caught in a seabed trap five hundred metres down.
Giant isopods patrol the dark ocean floor, down to two thousand five hundred metres, eating whatever sinks: fish, squid, even whales.
These armoured cleaners help digest the ocean’s leftovers.
For forty years, its label used a cousin’s name.
It even starred in a sea-giants exhibition.
Everyone saw it; nobody saw it.
Then a researcher and the curator wheeled it into an X-ray scanner.
The scans, with tiny details of mouth and shell, proved it was a new species.
Its closest relative lives near Mexico’s Yucatán coast.
Its name joins its two homes: its birth island, and the town of its recognition.
You need no ship or submarine to find a new species.
Sometimes it sits on a shelf, hiding in plain sight, waiting for someone to look twice.
Here’s today’s idiom: "hiding in plain sight." If something is hiding in plain sight, everyone can see it, but nobody notices it — like a new species sitting on a museum shelf for forty years!
Here’s an example: "The keys were hiding in plain sight, on the kitchen table." What treasure might be hiding in plain sight in your home?
Let's think about today's stories.
A crocodile hid in a museum for a hundred years, and a sea giant for forty.
Now, two questions for you.
First: if you could peek inside one museum drawer, what would you hope to find?
Second: what thing in your home deserves a second look?
Talk about it with your family!
That's all for today, young explorers.
Keep your eyes open, look twice — a treasure may be hiding in plain sight!
See you tomorrow morning!
